newsitem.title: USA: Courtroom solemn as Oklahoma bomb verdict read.
newsitem.headline: Courtroom solemn as Oklahoma bomb verdict read.

text.p: It was a moment of silent weeping.
The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial warned spectators in the courtroom on Monday he would not tolerate any outburst when the verdict was read, so many of them wept silently.

As Federal Judge Richard Matsch solemnly read the jury's guilty verdicts against Timothy McVeigh, spectators in the packed courtroom, many of whom had lost relatives in the blast that killed 168 people, started sobbing. Tears streamed down their faces, but nobody said a word.
The 29-year-old McVeigh showed no emotion, positioning himself in such a way that his face was partially covered by his hands and turned toward Judge Matsch so the spectators could not see him.

The jury had their eyes downcast as if to avoid looking at McVeigh, who they had found guilty of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, in the worst attack on civilians in U.S. history.

Jannie Coverdale, whose young grandsons Elijah and Aaron were killed in the day care centre in the Murrah building, sat motionless with her eyes closed as though she was praying when the verdict was read.

McVeigh, found guilty on all 11 counts of murder, bombing and conspiracy, could now face the death penalty. The former soldier sat perfectly still. He looked intently at the judge during the short 15-minute proceeding, then shook hands with his lead attorney Stephen Jones just before being escorted out of the courtroom by three marshals.
After the judge excused the jury, relatives started smiling, embracing and giving each other the thumbs up sign.
U.S. marshals warned the swarm of journalists running out of the courtroom to slow down.
But while the mood in the courtroom was solemn, it was quite a different picture outside.
Hundreds of onlookers had assembled outside the downtown Denver courthouse and cheered and applauded when the prosecution team, led by Joseph Hartzler in his wheelchair, emerged from the courthouse.

Outside, hundreds of reporters, photographers and television crews scrambled for interviews with lawyers and relatives of victims. Television production assistants tugged at the arms of relatives, fighting to get them on live television for their network first.

Police officers formed a line in front of the court and officers in cars and on horseback patrolled the area. A young man was arrested after shouting at a relative that the children of Waco did not get justice.
Prosecutors alleged McVeigh bombed the federal building to avenge 80 Branch Davidian cult members killed in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco, Texas, exactly two years earlier.
Within 90 minutes of the verdict being read, the Rocky Mountain News, a Denver newspaper, had an "extra" edition on the streets, proclaiming in huge black letters "Guilty" over a mugshot of McVeigh.
